deities: Lord Shiva as Kapaleeshwarar (Lord of the Skull, referencing Shiva holding Brahma's skull)
Goddess Parvati as Karpagambal (goddess of blessings)
Subshrines: Nataraja, Ganesha, Murugan and others
festivals: Panguni Brahmotsavam / Peruvizha (March-April; 10 days, with chariot processions)
Arubathimoovar (procession of the 63 Shaivite Nayanar saints, during Panguni)

history.period: Original 7th century CE (Pallava); current structure 16th century (Vijayanagara)
history.summary: One of Chennai's most famous temples, located in Mylapore (Mylai). The temple is believed to have been built in the 7th century by the Pallava rulers; the original seaside structure was destroyed by the Portuguese, and the current Dravidian-style temple was rebuilt in the 16th century by the Vijayanagara kings (with Nayak contributions). Dedicated to Lord Shiva as Kapaleeshwarar and Parvati as Karpagambal, the name derives from Shiva holding Brahma's skull (kapalam) as punishment. Legend holds that Parvati worshipped Shiva here in the form of a peahen (mayil), giving Mylapore its name (Mayilapur, city of peacocks) and Mylapore's older name Mayurapuri. The towering Rajagopuram (~37-40 m / 120 ft) is covered in vividly coloured stucco figures of deities, mythological scenes and the 63 Nayanmar saints; the Shiva lingam in the sanctum faces west (rare in Tamil Nadu) and is described as swayambhu (self-manifested) in some accounts (verify). The temple tank (pushkarini) hosts the float festival, and the sacred Punnai tree remains a focal point for devotees. One of the Sapta Sthana (seven sacred) Shiva temples of Mylapore-area tradition (verify).

name: Kapaleeshwarar Temple
town_description: Mylapore is Chennai's oldest and most culturally significant neighbourhood, the historic centre of Tamil Brahmin and temple culture. The Kapaleeshwarar Temple sits at 234, Ramakrishna Mutt Road, Mylapore, Chennai 600004, about 2.5 km from Marina Beach and 7-8 km from Chennai Central station, easily accessible via Mylapore MRTS station and local buses. The surrounding streets form a traditional agraharam quarter with flower, music and craft shops.

travel.railway: Chennai Central - about 7-8 km; Mylapore MRTS station is the nearest rail stop.
travel.road: On Ramakrishna Mutt Road, Mylapore; well served by city buses, metro and auto-rickshaws (verify).

visitor_information.best_time: November to February (cooler months); the Arubathimoovar festival in March-April offers a unique cultural experience but expect large crowds.
visitor_information.opening_hours: Typically 6:00 AM-12:30 PM and 4:30 PM-9:30 PM daily (varies slightly by day and festival; some sources say 5:00 AM-12:00 PM and 4:00 PM-9:00 PM - verify). No entry fee; special poojas and abhishekams carry fees. Modest dress covering shoulders and knees is expected.
